teaser: The model for this Christ still hangs in a small Breton chapel. It was never yellow.
review_notes:
1889 situation: Volpini exhibition at the Café des Arts during the Exposition Universelle, no sales; Gauguin living on credit at the Gloanec inn in Pont-Aven and then at Le Pouldu: standard account.
Mette and the five children in Copenhagen since 1885: correct.
Model: 17th-century polychrome wooden crucifix in the Trémalo chapel near Pont-Aven, still in place.
The small figure at right is usually described as a man climbing over a wall or stile; the two pale shapes beyond are read as two women.
Self-Portrait with the Yellow Christ, Musée d'Orsay, 1890-91: the Christ appears reversed because Gauguin painted himself in a mirror.
Acquired by the Albright Art Gallery (now Buffalo AKG) in 1946.
Quote 'I love Brittany. I find the wild and the primitive here' is from an 1888 letter to Schuffenecker.
The Green Christ (Breton Calvary), 1889, Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, based on the stone calvary at Nizon.
Dimensions about 92 x 73 cm.

lesson.text: By 1889 Paul Gauguin had almost nothing. Six years earlier he had been a Paris stockbroker with a comfortable income. Now his wife Mette was in Copenhagen with their five children, living near her family, and he was running up a bill at a country inn in Brittany. That summer he showed his work in a café beside the Paris World's Fair. Nothing sold.

Brittany was cheap, which was one reason he stayed. The other was what he believed he found there: an old, stubborn, deeply Catholic world of stone chapels and roadside crosses. “I love Brittany,” he wrote. “I find the wild and the primitive here.” In the autumn he painted this, a crucifixion set not in Jerusalem but in the fields outside Pont-Aven.

The figure is copied from a real object. In the chapel of Trémalo, a short walk above Pont-Aven, a painted wooden Christ carved in the 1600s hangs on the wall. It is still there today. Its body is a pale ivory color, not yellow.

So the yellow is Gauguin's decision. He took the color of the hills in October, when the wheat is cut and the trees turn rust red, and poured it into the body. Christ and countryside become the same substance. Around the cross sit three women in local dress, as calm as if they were resting after a day's work.

lesson.title: A carved god, three farm women
lesson.text: Follow how Gauguin simplifies everything he touches.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Eyes closed, mouth small, a few dark lines for the brow and beard. No blood, no agony. It has the plain, stiff look of the folk carving it was copied from.

spots.title: The body
spots.text: A thin blue-green outline runs around the whole figure. Inside it the yellow is nearly flat, with only a little green to hint at ribs and knees.

spots.title: The kneeling women
spots.text: White caps, a blue dress, an orange apron, hands folded in the lap. Their faces are lowered. They sit in a ring around the cross the way villagers gather at a wayside shrine.

spots.title: Seen from behind
spots.text: The third woman turns her back to you. Her pink-gray cap and shoulders make a soft mound at the bottom edge. You look over her shoulder, as part of the circle.

lesson.text: Are these women at the real Crucifixion? Clearly not. They are Bretons of 1889, and what stands before them is their own faith, made visible in their own fields. Gauguin had tried the same idea a year earlier with a vision set on bright red ground. Here he makes it quieter: no miracle, only a habit of prayer so old it has become part of the land.
Gauguin used color for feeling, not for likeness: one yellow joins a suffering body to an autumn harvest.
Not everyone in the picture is praying, though. The middle distance holds a small scene that has nothing holy about it, and it changes the mood of the whole painting once you notice it.
Someone is leaving. Find the figure walking away from the cross.

spots.title: Over the wall
spots.text: A man in dark blue swings his leg over a low stone wall. Just past him, two pale shapes look like women in caps. Life goes on in the next field, with its back to the cross.

lesson.text: That little escape is what keeps the picture from being a simple devotional image. Gauguin was not a churchgoer. He was an outsider watching other people believe, and half envying them. The climbing man might be anyone, a farmhand heading home. He might also be the painter's own restlessness, already looking for the way out.

Gauguin liked this canvas enough to put it in a self-portrait. In a painting now at the Musée d'Orsay in Paris, his head sits in front of the Yellow Christ. The crucifixion appears flipped left to right, because he was looking at himself, and the picture behind him, in a mirror.

The signature in the bottom right corner reads “P Gauguin 89.” Less than two years later he sold what he could at auction and sailed for Tahiti, convinced that Brittany was no longer wild enough. The painting itself crossed the Atlantic and has belonged to the museum in Buffalo, New York, since 1946.
The Yellow Christ has a sibling. The same year Gauguin painted a “Green Christ,” based on a mossy stone carving that stands outdoors beside a church near Pont-Aven. That one is now in Brussels.

quiz.question: What was Gauguin's situation in 1889?
options: He was nearly broke, living on credit in Brittany
He was teaching at an art school
quiz.explanation: He had left finance years earlier, and his café exhibition that summer sold nothing.

quiz.question: What is the Christ figure based on?
options: A wooden crucifix in a chapel near Pont-Aven
A Renaissance painting in the Louvre
quiz.explanation: Gauguin copied a carved Christ from the 1600s in the Trémalo chapel.

quiz.question: Where does the yellow come from?
quiz.explanation: The carving is ivory colored; Gauguin gave the body the color of the October fields.

quiz.question: What is the small man in the background doing?
options: Climbing over a wall, walking away
Carrying a ladder to the cross
quiz.explanation: He steps over a stone wall with his back to the cross.

quiz.question: Why is the Yellow Christ reversed in Gauguin's self-portrait?
options: He painted what he saw in a mirror
quiz.explanation: The mirror flipped both his face and the canvas behind him.

facts.text: The wooden crucifix Gauguin copied was destroyed long ago.
facts.explanation: It still hangs in the Trémalo chapel above Pont-Aven.

facts.text: The three women wear the dress of Breton villagers of Gauguin's own time.
facts.explanation: They are local women of 1889, not figures from the Bible story.

facts.text: Gauguin painted this picture in Tahiti.
facts.explanation: He painted it in Brittany in 1889, before he ever left for Tahiti.
